name: Busoa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source.
catalog_citation: van den Berg, René. 2020. The Busoa language of Southeast Sulawesi: Grammar sketch, texts, vocabulary. SIL Language and Culture Documentation and Description 48. Dallas: SIL International. ISSN 1939-0785.
catalog_quote: Stress is predictable in Busoa; it is assigned to the penultimate syllable of the word, irrespective of the position of the root in the word. Secondary stress appears to occur on every second syllable preceding the stressed syllable. In the following examples primary stress is marked by the raised stress mark <ˈ> preceding the stressed syllable, while secondary stress is indicated by the lowered stress mark <ˌ>. pandanga /pɑˈndɑŋɑ/ ‘spear’ pandanga-no /pɑⁿdɑˈŋɑnɔ/ ‘his spear’ pandanga-no-mo /pɑˌⁿdɑŋɑˈnɔmɔ/ ‘it is his spear’ pande /ˈpɑndɛ/ ‘clever, able’ no-pande /nɔˈpɑⁿdɛ/ ‘he/she is able’ no-pande-mo /ˌnɔpɑˈⁿdɛmɔ/ ‘he/she is already able’ mbeli-mbeli /ˌᵐbɛliˈᵐbɛli/ ‘go for a walk’ sa-no-fe-mbeli-mbeli-mo /ˌsɑnɔˌfɛᵐbɛˌliᵐbɛˈlimɔ/ ‘he keeps on walking’ The only complication regarding stress is with syllables without a consonantal onset in non-final position. It appears that the two vowels in such CVV sequences (e.g. lou in a-lou-mo ‘I have gone down’) are treated as a single vowel for stress purposes, but this is only the case if the second vowel is higher than the first one. In other words, words containing the sequences ai, ae, ao, au, oi, ou, ei, eu in antepenultimate and penultimate position have the stress on the antepenultimate vowel.

new_statements.citation: van den Berg, René. 2020. The Busoa language of Southeast Sulawesi: Grammar sketch, texts, vocabulary. SIL Language and Culture Documentation and Description 48. Dallas: SIL International.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (PDF v1.4, text, author metadata 'René van den Berg', title 'Busoa Grammar, Texts, and Vocabulary'; present listing SIL LCDD 48 URL + Internet Archive copy). extracted text of pp. 50-51 (printed pp. 28-29) shows §2.8 'Stress' exactly as quoted: 'Stress is predictable in Busoa; it is assigned to the penultimate syllable of the word, irrespective of the position of the root in the word. Secondary stress appears to occur on every second syllable preceding the stressed syllable.' followed (after the example block with pandanga /pɑˈndɑŋɑ/, pandanga-no /pɑndɑˈŋɑnɔ/, pandanga-no-mo /pɑˌndɑŋɑˈnɔmɔ/, sa-no-fe-mbeli-mbeli-mo /ˌsɑnɔˌfɛmbɛˌlimbɛˈlimɔ/) by 'The only complication regarding stress is…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the (morphologically complex) word, shifting rightward as suffixes/enclitics are added (pandanga /pɑˈndɑŋɑ/, pandanga-no /pɑndɑˈŋɑnɔ/, pandanga-no-mo /pɑˌndɑŋɑˈnɔmɔ/); the minimal word is a disyllabic trochee.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress 'appears to occur on every second syllable preceding the stressed syllable' (alternating leftward), e.g. /ˌsɑnɔˌfɛmbɛˌlimbɛˈlimɔ/.
new_statements.exceptions: When the antepenult+penult form a vowel sequence whose second vowel is higher than the first (ai, ae, ao, au, oi, ou, ei, eu), or a sequence of identical vowels (laano /ˈlɑ:nɔ/), the two vowels count as one stress unit and stress surfaces on the antepenultimate vowel (aloumo /ɑˈloumɔ/, bhaemu /ˈɓɑemu/); word-final such sequences behave regularly (alou /ɑˈlou/). Author treats this as a post-lexical desyllabification rule.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including suffixes and enclitics (examples show =mo, -no shifting stress); examples are citation forms in phonemic transcription. Stress is non-contrastive/predictable.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Busoa [bup] = buso1238 as spoken in Busoa village, southwest Buton; author states there are no known dialects (a near-extinct Wuragana variant differs only in minor morphology/lexicon). No identity mismatch.

sources.note: §2.8 Stress (pp. 28-29): stress is predictable, on the penultimate syllable of the word irrespective of root position; secondary stress on every second syllable preceding the primary; exception: rising vowel sequences (ai, ae, ao, au, oi, ou, ei, eu) and identical-vowel sequences in antepenult+penult position count as one stress unit, giving stress on the antepenultimate vowel (e.g. /ɑˈloumɔ/, /ˈɓɑemu/). §2.7 also: minimal word is a trochaic foot with penultimate stress. §1.3 states there are no earlier studies of Busoa (only Kaseng et al. 1987 wordlist, van den Berg 1991, 2003 mentions).
